title: Monitoring functions related to health and welfare status of aquatic organisms, etc.

lessons.title: Monitoring health and welfare on the job
lessons.html:
Your responsibility in the workplace

In this work experience you take charge of health and welfare monitoring for assigned units under a mentor. The goal is to show that you can detect problems early, respond correctly and keep complete records over a sustained period.

Daily monitoring tasks

  • Observe every assigned unit at feeding and score the feeding response.
  • Note abnormal behaviour: gasping, flashing, crowding at inflows, lethargy, erratic swimming.
  • Note physical signs: spots, ulcers, fin damage, fungal growths, eye or belly swelling, gill colour.
  • Remove, count and record mortalities and moribund fish.
  • Check water quality readings for the same units and link them to what you see.
  • Check welfare factors: stocking density, handling practices, shade or covers, predator protection.

Weekly tasks

  • Review the mortality trend for each unit.
  • Check that treatment records are complete and withdrawal dates are marked on unit cards.
  • Inspect biosecurity: foot baths, dedicated equipment, quarantine practices.
  • Discuss findings with your mentor.

Escalation

Know the farm's escalation rules: what you handle yourself (for example, correcting low oxygen by starting backup aeration), what you report to your supervisor the same day, and what triggers an immediate call to the vet. A sudden rise in deaths, unusual signs across several units, or signs of a possible notifiable disease must be escalated without delay.

Sampling for diagnosis

When the vet requests samples, select fresh moribund fish showing typical signs, keep them as instructed (often chilled, not frozen, unless told otherwise), label with unit, date and signs, and deliver promptly. Record what was sent and when.

Safety

Wear gloves when handling sick or dead fish and wash hands afterwards. Use protective equipment with treatments. Follow the farm's procedure for disposing of dead fish.

lessons.title: Recording, reporting and evidence
lessons.html:
Records that tell a story

Health records are only useful if they are complete, consistent and reviewed. In your workplace placement, your records are also your main evidence.

Records to maintain

RecordFrequency
Daily health and feeding log per unitDaily
Mortality registerDaily
Water quality logAs scheduled
Treatment register with withdrawal datesEach treatment
Vet visits and sample submissionsEach event
Biosecurity checksDaily or weekly

Writing a health report

When something goes wrong, write a short report:

  1. What was observed, where and when.
  2. Water quality at the time.
  3. Actions taken immediately.
  4. Who was informed and their instructions.
  5. Outcome over the following days.
  6. Lessons and preventive changes.

Using trends

Plot daily mortalities per unit over weeks. Mark events on the chart: grading, transport, treatments, heat waves, power failures. Patterns appear, for example losses rising about a week after grading, which point to changes in practice.

Evidence for assessment

  • Your completed logs and registers, signed by your mentor.
  • Observation checklists completed by the mentor.
  • Health reports you wrote on real incidents.
  • Reflection notes on what you learned.

Evidence must be your own work, current and sufficient to show consistent performance.

Welfare mindset

Monitoring is not only about losses. Ask every day whether fish are kept in conditions that let them behave normally with minimal stress: clean water, space, gentle handling and humane culling. Raise welfare concerns with your mentor.

Key points

  • Observe every unit daily at feeding and record signs and mortalities.
  • Link behaviour to water quality readings.
  • Follow escalation rules; call the vet promptly for sudden or unusual losses.
  • Keep complete treatment records with withdrawal dates.
  • Use mortality trends and incident reports to improve practice.

quiz.question: Which situation should trigger an immediate call to the vet?

options.text: One fish with a small scratch
A sudden rise in deaths across several units
A routine water reading in range

quiz.question: Which fish should be sent for diagnosis?

options.text: Fresh moribund fish showing typical signs
Any fish, it does not matter

quiz.question: What is the first item in a health incident report?

options.text: What was observed, where and when

quiz.question: Why mark events like grading on a mortality chart?

options.text: To reveal patterns linking losses to practices

quiz.question: What should you do after handling dead fish?
Health monitoring includes checking welfare factors like stocking density and handling.
Treatment records do not need withdrawal dates if the fish look healthy.
